short: A central bank shrinking its pile of bought bonds, usually by not reinvesting them as they mature, which pulls money out of the financial system.
kid: A grown-up once handed out lots of extra sweets so the party would be fun. Now the party is too wild, so each week the grown-up quietly collects a few sweets back.
detail: Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of quantitative easing. A central bank that bought government bonds and mortgage securities with newly created reserves now reduces those holdings, either passively, by letting bonds mature without reinvesting the proceeds, or actively, by selling them, as the Bank of England has done with gilts. Each bond that runs off removes reserves from the banking system and hands more interest-rate risk back to private investors, which tends to push up longer-term yields and tighten financial conditions alongside rate hikes. The US Federal Reserve ran QT from June 2022, slowed it in 2024 and 2025, and ended the runoff on 1 December 2025. The RBI has no formal QT programme, though its open market sales of bonds drain rupee liquidity in a similar way. Confusion to avoid: QT is not tapering, which only slows new purchases.
example: Under its 2022 plan, the Fed let up to $60 billion of Treasuries and $35 billion of mortgage-backed securities mature each month without reinvesting. That is up to $95 billion a month, or $95 billion × 12 = $1.14 trillion over a full year at the maximum pace.
formula: Monthly runoff = Maturing securities not reinvested, up to the monthly cap

short: A central bank gradually slowing the pace of its new bond purchases under quantitative easing, step by step, before stopping them altogether.
kid: A parent who gave you ten sweets a day starts giving nine, then eight, then seven. You still get sweets for a while, just fewer each day, until they stop.
detail: Tapering is the wind-down phase of quantitative easing (QE). The central bank keeps buying bonds but cuts the monthly amount in steps, usually signalled well in advance, until purchases reach zero. Because it is still buying, its balance sheet keeps growing during a taper; shrinking starts only with quantitative tightening. Markets watch tapering closely because rate hikes often follow. In May 2013, Fed Chair Ben Bernanke merely hinted at tapering, US yields jumped and money rushed out of emerging markets: this 'taper tantrum' pushed the rupee to a record low near 68.8 per dollar in August 2013 and put India among the 'Fragile Five'. The Fed then tapered through 2014, and again from November 2021 to March 2022. Confusion to avoid: tapering means slowing purchases, not selling bonds or raising rates.
example: In November 2021 the Fed was buying $120 billion of bonds a month and announced cuts of $15 billion a month, a pace that would have reached zero in $120 billion / $15 billion = 8 months. In December it doubled the cut to $30 billion a month, and buying ended in March 2022.
formula: Months to finish = Current monthly purchases / Monthly reduction

short: A record of what a central bank owns, like bonds, foreign currency and gold, and what it owes, mainly printed notes and banks' deposits.
kid: A big keeper of coins writes two lists in a notebook. One list shows everything she holds, and the other shows everything she has promised to others. The two lists always come out equal.
detail: A central bank's balance sheet shows its assets, typically government bonds, foreign exchange reserves, gold and loans to banks, and its liabilities, mainly currency in circulation, commercial banks' reserves, government deposits and funds absorbed through reverse repo operations. Because a central bank creates its own currency, buying an asset simply creates a matching liability: when it buys bonds, bank reserves rise by the same amount. Its size therefore tracks policy. The Fed's balance sheet grew from about $0.9 trillion before 2008 to nearly $9 trillion in 2022 through QE, then shrank under quantitative tightening. The RBI's balance sheet, which runs on an April-March year, is dominated by foreign assets and rupee securities, and its surplus is transferred to the government. Confusion to avoid: a bigger balance sheet means more reserves in the banking system, not necessarily more lending to households and firms.
example: Say the RBI buys ₹20,000 crore of government bonds from banks through an open market operation. Its assets rise by ₹20,000 crore of bonds and its liabilities rise by the same ₹20,000 crore as the sellers' reserve balances are credited, so the balance sheet grows by ₹20,000 crore on both sides.
formula: Total assets = Currency in circulation + Bank reserves + Other liabilities + Capital and reserves

short: A US Federal Reserve chart in which each policymaker marks with a dot the interest rate they think right for each coming year-end.
kid: Each grown-up in a group puts a sticker on a chart to show how many sweets they think the class should get next year. You look at where most stickers sit to guess what will happen.
detail: The dot plot is part of the Federal Reserve's Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), released after four of the eight FOMC meetings each year, in March, June, September and December. Each of up to 19 participants, the seven Board governors and twelve regional Fed presidents, anonymously places one dot for the federal funds rate they judge appropriate at the end of the current year, the next few years and the longer run. Markets focus on the median dot and how it shifts from the previous quarter, comparing it with the rate path priced in futures. Indian traders watch it because a higher US path tends to strengthen the dollar and pull foreign money out of emerging markets. Confusion to avoid: the dots are individual views, not a committee forecast or a promise, and they include presidents who do not vote that year.
example: Say 19 year-end dots, sorted from lowest to highest, are 6 at 3.375%, 4 at 3.625% and 9 at 3.875%. The median is the 10th dot, which is 3.625%, the midpoint of a 3.50%-3.75% fed funds target range.
formula: Median dot = middle value of all participants' dots (the 10th of 19 when sorted)

short: A Federal Reserve report, published eight times a year, summarising what businesses and contacts across its 12 regional districts say about the US economy.
kid: Twelve friends each ask the shopkeepers on their street how things are going. Then they put all the stories in one little book so everyone can read it.
detail: The Beige Book, formally the Summary of Commentary on Current Economic Conditions, is released about two weeks before each of the eight FOMC meetings a year. Each of the 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks gathers anecdotes from businesses, bankers, economists and community groups in its district on hiring, wages, prices, spending and lending, and the reports are combined with a national summary. It is qualitative rather than statistical, so its value lies in early, ground-level signals, such as firms reporting cooling demand or rising input costs, before official data confirm them. Markets read the tone of words like 'slight', 'modest' or 'flat'. The name comes from its cover. Confusion to avoid: it describes current conditions; it is not a policy decision or a forecast. India has no direct equivalent, though RBI surveys such as the Industrial Outlook Survey play a similar listening role.
example: Say a Beige Book reports that 8 of the 12 districts saw slight growth, 3 saw no change and 1 saw a mild decline. With two-thirds of districts (8 out of 12) growing only slightly, readers would see a modestly expanding economy rather than a boom.

short: The published written record of a central bank's rate-setting meeting, showing the arguments members made and, in India's case, how each member voted.
kid: After a group of friends decide which game to play, one of them writes down what everyone said. Later, others can read the notes to see who wanted what.
detail: Minutes reveal the debate behind a rate decision, so markets use them to judge how united a committee is and where policy may head next. Under the RBI Act, the RBI must publish its Monetary Policy Committee minutes on the fourteenth day after each meeting; they include every member's vote and a statement explaining it, so a 4-2 split can be traced to named members. The US Federal Open Market Committee releases minutes three weeks after each decision; they describe what 'participants', 'several' or 'a few' argued without naming them, though the vote and any dissents are recorded. The Bank of England publishes its minutes with the decision, and the ECB releases an 'account' about four weeks later. Confusion to avoid: minutes are an edited summary, not a transcript; the Fed releases full transcripts only after five years.
example: Say the RBI's MPC announces its decision on 6 June; the minutes then come out on 20 June, 14 days later. If they show a 4-2 vote with the two dissenters wanting a 25 basis point cut, traders may price a higher chance of a cut at the next meeting.

short: An annual late-August conference of central bankers and economists in Wyoming, USA, hosted by the Kansas City Fed, where big policy signals are often given.
kid: Once a year, the grown-ups who look after a country's coins meet in a valley by the mountains. Everyone listens closely in case they hint at what they will do next.
detail: The Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium has been hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City since 1978 and held in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, each August since 1982 (online in 2020 and 2021). Central bank governors, finance officials and academics discuss papers on a chosen theme, but markets care most about the Fed Chair's keynote, which has often been used to signal shifts. Ben Bernanke laid the ground for a second round of QE there in 2010; Jerome Powell unveiled average inflation targeting in 2020, gave a short, blunt warning of further rate hikes in 2022, and said in 2024 that the time had come for policy to adjust, ahead of the first cut. Bonds, the dollar and emerging-market currencies, including the rupee, often swing around the speech. Confusion to avoid: no rate decision is taken there; the FOMC still decides at its scheduled meetings.
example: On 26 August 2022, Powell's roughly eight-minute Jackson Hole speech warned that bringing inflation down would bring some pain to households and businesses, and the S&P 500 fell about 3.4% that day. For an investor holding $10,000 in an S&P 500 index fund, that was a one-day loss of about $10,000 × 3.4% = $340.

short: The US central bank's main policy rate: the overnight rate at which banks lend each other spare cash held at the Federal Reserve.
kid: When one child has spare crayons and another needs some until tomorrow, they share. A grown-up decides roughly how many extra crayons should come back as a thank-you.
detail: The federal funds rate is the rate on unsecured overnight loans of reserve balances between US banks and other eligible institutions. The Federal Open Market Committee sets a target range 25 basis points wide, and the New York Fed publishes the effective federal funds rate (EFFR), the volume-weighted median of actual trades. With reserves plentiful, the Fed keeps the rate in its range mainly through administered rates, interest on reserve balances and the overnight reverse repo rate, rather than by adjusting reserves daily. The rate anchors dollar borrowing costs worldwide, and changes in it move the dollar and foreign flows into India. Between March 2022 and July 2023 the Fed raised the range from 0-0.25% to 5.25-5.50%; for the current range, see the live rates board. Confusion to avoid: it is not the rate consumers pay, though prime, card and loan rates follow it.
example: Say a bank borrows $100 million overnight in the fed funds market at 5.33%. Using the market's actual/360 convention, it pays $100,000,000 × 5.33% / 360 = about $14,806 in interest for that one night.
formula: Overnight interest = Amount borrowed × Fed funds rate × 1/360

short: The rate the Federal Reserve pays banks on money they keep in their accounts at the Fed; its main tool for steering short-term rates.
kid: If you leave your toys in the teacher's cupboard overnight, she gives you a sticker for each one. If her stickers are good, you won't lend your toys to anyone else for less.
detail: Interest on reserve balances (IORB) is the rate the Federal Reserve pays on balances that banks hold in their Fed accounts. The Fed began paying interest on reserves in October 2008, first through separate rates on required and excess reserves (IORR and IOER), merged into a single IORB rate in July 2021. Since QE made reserves abundant, IORB has been the Fed's main tool: a bank will rarely lend reserves to others for less than it can earn risk-free at the Fed, so IORB pulls market rates such as the fed funds rate toward it. The Fed usually sets it inside the target range, a little below the top. When rates rose sharply after 2022, IORB payments exceeded the Fed's income on its bonds, producing operating losses. Confusion to avoid: IORB is a policy tool, not a reward for lending; in India the RBI pays no interest on CRR balances.
example: Say a bank keeps $2 billion in its Fed account and IORB is 4.40%. Over a year it earns $2,000,000,000 × 4.40% = $88 million, so it has no reason to lend those funds overnight to another bank at, say, 4.30%.
formula: Annual interest earned = Reserve balance × IORB rate

short: A Federal Reserve facility where money market funds and others lend cash to the Fed overnight at a set rate, with Treasury bonds as security.
kid: Some children have spare sweets at bedtime. They can give them to the teacher overnight and get them back in the morning with one extra sweet as a thank-you.
detail: In an ON RRP trade, an eligible counterparty, mainly money market funds but also government-sponsored enterprises, banks and primary dealers, gives cash to the Fed overnight and receives Treasury securities, which the Fed buys back the next day at a slightly higher price. The offering rate is set at the bottom of the fed funds target range, so it acts as a floor: a money fund will not lend to anyone else for less than it gets from the Fed. Usage swelled above $2.5 trillion at the end of 2022, when excess cash from QE had few other homes, then fell steeply as Treasury bill supply rose and QT drained liquidity. Analysts watch the balance as a gauge of surplus dollar liquidity. Confusion to avoid: 'reverse repo' is named from the Fed's side; the fund is effectively lending. India's closest analogue is the RBI's standing deposit facility.
example: Say a money market fund places $1 billion in the ON RRP facility for one night at 4.25%. It earns $1,000,000,000 × 4.25% / 360 = about $118,056 and gets its $1 billion back the next morning.
formula: Overnight interest = Cash placed × ON RRP rate × 1/360

short: The Federal Reserve's lending counter where banks can borrow directly from the Fed for short periods by pledging assets, a backstop when funding dries up.
kid: If a shop runs out of coins to give change, it can borrow some from a big helper next door, leaving a toy as a promise. It gives the coins back soon and gets its toy back.
detail: The discount window lets US banks and other depository institutions borrow from their regional Federal Reserve Bank against collateral such as Treasuries, mortgages and business loans. Primary credit, for financially sound banks, is offered overnight or for up to 90 days at the primary credit rate, which since March 2020 has been set at the top of the fed funds target range; secondary and seasonal credit serve weaker and smaller banks. It acts as a ceiling on short-term rates and a liquidity backstop: after Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, primary credit borrowing hit a record of about $153 billion in one week. Its weakness is stigma, since banks fear that borrowing signals trouble, one reason the Fed added a standing repo facility. India's closest equivalent is the RBI's marginal standing facility. Confusion to avoid: the name is historical; today it is collateralised lending, not discounting of bills.
example: Say a sound bank borrows $500 million overnight at a primary credit rate of 4.50%, pledging $600 million of loans as collateral. It pays $500,000,000 × 4.50% / 360 = $62,500 in interest and repays the next day.
formula: Interest cost = Amount borrowed × Primary credit rate × Days / 360

short: The rate the European Central Bank pays, or charges when negative, on banks' overnight deposits with it; since 2024 its main policy rate.
kid: Children can leave spare marbles with the head teacher overnight. Usually she adds a marble as a thank-you, but for a few years she asked for one back instead.
detail: The deposit facility rate (DFR) is one of three ECB key rates, alongside the main refinancing rate and the marginal lending facility rate. Because euro-area banks hold large excess liquidity after years of asset purchases, short-term market rates such as the euro short-term rate (€STR) trade just below the DFR, so it effectively sets the price of money. The ECB recognised this in its March 2024 framework review and now signals its stance through the DFR, with the main refinancing rate set 15 basis points above it from September 2024. The DFR was negative from June 2014 to July 2022, bottoming at -0.50%, then rose to 4.00% by September 2023; for the current level, see the live rates board. Confusion to avoid: headlines once quoted the refi rate as 'the ECB rate', but today the deposit rate is the one that steers euro money markets.
example: Say a bank keeps €100 million of excess cash at the ECB for a whole year. At a DFR of 2.00% it earns €100,000,000 × 2.00% = €2 million; at the -0.50% rate in force from 2019 to 2022 it would instead have paid the ECB €100,000,000 × 0.50% = €500,000, before any tiering exemption.
formula: Annual interest = Excess deposits × Deposit facility rate

short: The rate at which euro-area banks borrow from the European Central Bank for one week by pledging assets; for years the ECB's headline rate.
kid: When a shop in a big town needs extra coins for a week, it can borrow them from the town's coin keeper. It leaves something valuable as a promise and returns the coins with a small extra.
detail: Main refinancing operations (MROs) are the ECB's regular one-week loans to banks, secured on eligible collateral such as government and corporate bonds. Since October 2008 they have been run at a fixed rate with full allotment, so banks get as much as they ask for at the MRO rate. Before 2008, liquidity was scarce and the MRO rate steered market rates, which is why it was quoted as 'the ECB rate'. Once asset purchases flooded the system with reserves, money market rates sank toward the deposit facility rate, and from September 2024 the MRO rate has been set just 15 basis points above the DFR. It sat at 0% from March 2016 to July 2022. Above it is the marginal lending facility rate, the overnight ceiling. For current levels, see the live rates board. Confusion to avoid: it is a refinancing rate for banks, not a mortgage refinancing rate.
example: Say a bank borrows €500 million in a one-week MRO at 3.00%. Interest is €500,000,000 × 3.00% × 7 / 360 = about €291,667, repaid with the €500 million a week later.
formula: Interest = Amount borrowed × MRO rate × Days / 360

short: The Bank of England's main policy rate, paid on money banks keep at the Bank and set by its nine-member Monetary Policy Committee.
kid: In one big country, a group of nine grown-ups decides how many extra sweets you get back for lending your sweets for a while. When they change their minds, everyone in the country notices.
detail: Bank Rate is the rate the Bank of England pays on reserve balances held by commercial banks, and it anchors sterling money markets, mortgage rates and savings rates across the UK. The nine-member Monetary Policy Committee, made up of the Governor, three Deputy Governors, the Chief Economist and four external members, votes at eight scheduled meetings a year, aiming at the 2% CPI inflation target set by the Chancellor. Each member's vote is published with the decision, so close splits are visible at once. Bank Rate fell to a record low of 0.1% in March 2020 and rose to 5.25% in August 2023, its highest since 2008; for today's level, see the live rates board. Confusion to avoid: the RBI also has a 'Bank Rate', a separate rate aligned with its marginal standing facility and used mainly for penalties, not India's policy repo rate.
example: Say a UK borrower has a £200,000 interest-only tracker mortgage at Bank Rate plus 1 percentage point. When Bank Rate was 0.1%, the yearly interest was £200,000 × 1.1% = £2,200; at 5.25%, it became £200,000 × 6.25% = £12,500.

short: A central bank policy of pinning the interest rate on a chosen government bond by promising to buy as much of it as needed.
kid: A shopkeeper says she will always buy your marbles for at least ten stickers each. Because she promises, nobody ever sells marbles for less than that.
detail: Under yield curve control (YCC), the central bank announces a target or ceiling for a specific bond yield and stands ready to buy unlimited amounts at the matching price. If the promise is credible, it may need to buy little, because investors will not sell below the price the bank defends. The Bank of Japan ran YCC from September 2016, holding the 10-year government bond yield around 0% within a band it widened in December 2022, loosened further in 2023 and scrapped in March 2024. The Reserve Bank of Australia targeted its 3-year yield in 2020-21, and the Fed capped yields during and after the Second World War. YCC keeps borrowing costs low, but it can force huge purchases, weaken the currency and end abruptly. Confusion to avoid: QE fixes the amount bought and lets yields float; YCC fixes the yield and lets the amount float.
example: In December 2022 the Bank of Japan widened its band for the 10-year government bond yield from plus or minus 0.25% to plus or minus 0.50%, doubling the ceiling it defended. For a 10-year zero-coupon bond with a face value of 100, the price is about 97.53 at a 0.25% yield and about 95.13 at 0.50%, so the change let prices fall by about 2.4.

short: A central bank setting its key rate below zero, so banks pay to keep spare money with it and are nudged to lend instead.
kid: Usually a friend gives you a little treat for minding your toys. Now imagine you had to give the friend a sweet instead, so you would rather let others play with them.
detail: Under a negative interest rate policy (NIRP), the central bank charges banks for holding excess reserves, aiming to lower borrowing costs, weaken the currency and encourage lending when rates are already near zero and inflation is too low. Denmark went negative in 2012 and the ECB in June 2014, its deposit rate reaching -0.50%, followed by Switzerland, Sweden and Japan, where the rate was -0.1% from 2016 to 2024. Negative policy rates helped push trillions of dollars of bonds worldwide to negative yields around 2019-20. The costs are squeezed bank margins, because banks rarely pass negative rates to ordinary depositors, and the risk that people hoard cash. Many central banks exempted part of banks' reserves through 'tiering' to ease the hit. India has never used negative rates. Confusion to avoid: a negative real rate, where inflation exceeds the nominal rate, is common; a negative nominal policy rate is rare.
example: Say a bank holds €1 billion of excess reserves at a central bank charging -0.50%. Over a year it pays €1,000,000,000 × 0.50% = €5 million, unless the money is lent out or exempted under a tiering system.
formula: Annual charge = Excess reserves × Negative deposit rate

short: The floor near zero below which a central bank cannot easily cut interest rates, because people could simply hold cash, which pays zero.
kid: If keeping your sweets in a jar meant losing some each week, you would just keep them in your pocket. So the jar keeper cannot take very many before everyone stops using the jar.
detail: The zero lower bound (ZLB) is the idea that nominal policy rates cannot go much below zero, because savers and banks can switch to physical cash, which earns exactly 0%. Experience in Europe and Japan showed rates can go slightly negative, since storing and insuring large amounts of cash is costly, so economists now often speak of an effective lower bound (ELB). The bound matters when a deep recession calls for a larger rate cut than is possible. The Fed held rates near zero from December 2008 to December 2015 and again from March 2020 to March 2022, relying instead on quantitative easing, forward guidance and lending programmes. India has stayed well clear: the RBI's lowest repo rate was 4.00%, in force from May 2020 to May 2022. Confusion to avoid: hitting the ZLB does not leave a central bank powerless; it changes which tools it uses.
example: Say inflation is 1% and the economy needs a real policy rate of -4%. The nominal rate required is -4% + 1% = -3%, but the central bank can cut only to about 0%, leaving roughly 3 percentage points of easing that must come from QE, forward guidance or government spending.
formula: Missing easing = Lower bound - Nominal rate the economy needs

short: The interest rate that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy when it is running at full capacity with stable inflation.
kid: Riding a bicycle downhill, you press the brakes; uphill, you pedal hard. The neutral spot is flat ground, where you neither brake nor push.
detail: The neutral rate, often written r*, is the real short-term interest rate consistent with output at its potential and inflation at target, so policy neither stimulates nor restrains demand. Adding expected inflation gives the nominal neutral rate. A policy rate above neutral is restrictive; below it, accommodative. The catch is that r* cannot be observed: it is estimated with models, such as Laubach-Williams in the US, and estimates shift with productivity, demographics, savings and global capital flows, with wide error bands. Estimates fell sharply after 2008, and whether they have risen since the pandemic is a live debate. The Fed's 'longer run' median dot is a rough guide to its officials' view of the nominal neutral rate, and RBI staff publish estimates for India. Confusion to avoid: neutral is a medium-term benchmark, not today's policy rate or the peak of a particular rate cycle.
example: Say India's real neutral rate is 1.5% and expected inflation is 4%. The nominal neutral rate is 1.5% + 4% = 5.5%, so a repo rate of 6.5% would be 1 percentage point above neutral, a restrictive stance.
formula: Nominal neutral rate = Real neutral rate (r*) + Expected inflation

short: A simple formula suggesting where a central bank's policy rate should be, based on how far inflation and output are from their targets.
kid: A simple recipe tells you how much to water a plant: more when the soil is dry, less when it is wet. This recipe does the same for deciding when to cool things down or warm them up.
detail: Proposed by economist John Taylor in 1993, the rule sets the nominal policy rate equal to the neutral real rate plus current inflation, plus half the gap between inflation and its target, plus half the output gap. If inflation runs above target or the economy runs hot, the rule calls for a higher rate; in a slump, a lower one. In its original form, with a 2% neutral rate and 2% inflation target, it closely tracked Fed policy in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Central banks, including the Fed, publish Taylor-type rules as cross-checks, and analysts use them to argue that policy is too loose or too tight, for instance that the Fed was behind the curve in 2021. Confusion to avoid: no central bank follows it mechanically, and its answer swings with the inputs chosen, especially uncertain estimates of the neutral rate and the output gap.
example: Say the neutral real rate is 2%, inflation is 3%, the target is 2% and output is 1% above potential. The rule gives 2% + 3% + 0.5 × (3% - 2%) + 0.5 × 1% = 6%, so a policy rate of 5% would look one percentage point too low.
formula: i = r* + π + 0.5 × (π - π*) + 0.5 × Output gap, where π is inflation and π* the inflation target

short: A way of running monetary policy in which the central bank publicly promises a numerical inflation goal and sets interest rates mainly to hit it.
kid: A teacher says the classroom should be just warm enough, not too hot and not too cold. Everyone knows the goal, so when it gets too hot she opens a window, and when it is too cold she closes it.
detail: Inflation targeting began in New Zealand in 1990 and is now used by most major central banks. The central bank announces a numerical target, explains its decisions against it and is held accountable when it misses. Most frameworks are 'flexible': they aim to bring inflation back to target over the medium term while giving weight to growth and jobs, rather than reacting to every monthly reading. The Fed targets 2% PCE inflation, the ECB and Bank of England 2%, and India adopted flexible inflation targeting in 2016, with a 4% CPI target and a 2% to 6% band under the framework in force as of 2025. A credible target anchors expectations: if people believe inflation will stay near target, wage and price setting follows, and smaller rate moves are needed. Confusion to avoid: the goal is steady inflation at target, not falling prices after a burst of inflation.
example: Say India's CPI index rises from 200 to 208 over a year. Inflation is (208 - 200) / 200 = 4%, exactly on the RBI's target under the framework as of 2025; a reading of 7% would sit above the 6% upper tolerance limit.
formula: Inflation = (CPI this year - CPI last year) / CPI last year × 100

short: The 2015 agreement between India's government and the RBI that made inflation control the RBI's main goal, with a 4% CPI target and 2-6% band.
kid: A school and its head teacher agree on one clear rule: the classroom should be comfortably warm. They even agree how much warmer or cooler is still fine before someone has to explain why.
detail: Signed on 20 February 2015 by the Finance Ministry and the RBI, the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement made price stability monetary policy's primary objective and set a glide path: CPI inflation below 6% by January 2016, then 4% with a band of plus or minus 2 percentage points. The Finance Act 2016 then wrote it into the RBI Act: the government sets the target in consultation with the RBI every five years, a six-member Monetary Policy Committee decides the repo rate, and inflation outside the 2-6% band for three consecutive quarters counts as a failure. The RBI must then report the reasons and its remedy to the government, as it first did in November 2022. The 4% target was set for 2016-21 and retained for 2021-26; check the current notification for later periods. Confusion to avoid: 4% is the target; 6% is only the upper tolerance limit.
example: With a 4% target and a band of 2 percentage points either side, the tolerable range runs from 4% - 2% = 2% to 4% + 2% = 6%. Say quarterly CPI inflation averages 6.3%, 7.0% and 6.4% in three straight quarters; all three are above 6%, so the RBI must write to the government explaining the miss.
formula: Tolerance band = Target ± 2 percentage points (4% ± 2% = 2% to 6%)

short: The US Federal Reserve's legal duty to pursue two goals at once: maximum employment and stable prices.
kid: A gardener has two jobs: keep every plant growing and never let the garden flood. Too much water makes things soggy and too little makes plants droop, so she balances both.
detail: Congress set the Fed's goals in the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977: maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates. Because stable prices tend to keep long-term rates moderate, the mandate is described as dual. The Fed interprets stable prices as 2% inflation on the PCE price index, while maximum employment has no fixed number and is judged from a wide range of labour-market data. Usually the goals point the same way: weak demand brings both low inflation and high unemployment. When they conflict, as with high inflation in a slowing economy, the Fed weighs which goal is further away and how fast each can return. Other central banks differ: the ECB's primary mandate is price stability, and the RBI's statutory objective is price stability while keeping growth in mind. Confusion to avoid: the dual mandate is not an unemployment target.
example: Say US inflation is 3.5%, or 3.5% - 2% = 1.5 percentage points above the goal, while unemployment is 4.0%, close to most estimates of maximum employment. The inflation side is further from target, so under the dual mandate the Fed would lean towards keeping rates higher for longer.

short: How a central bank's change in its policy rate flows through to loan and deposit rates, spending, prices and the wider economy.
kid: When you push the first domino, the rest fall one by one. Some fall quickly and some are slow, but the push travels all the way to the end.
detail: Transmission is the chain from a policy rate change to the real economy. Channels include interest rates on loans and deposits, the availability of credit, asset prices such as bonds and shares, the exchange rate, and expectations of future inflation. Money markets react within days and bond yields often move before the decision itself, but bank lending rates, spending and inflation adjust over several quarters, the 'long and variable lags' central bankers cite. In India, transmission was historically slow because loans were priced off internal benchmarks such as the base rate and MCLR, and deposit costs adjusted gradually. Since October 2019, new floating-rate retail and small-business loans must be linked to an external benchmark, usually the repo rate, and reset at least every three months. Confusion to avoid: transmission to new loans is faster than to existing ones, and slow-moving deposit rates often limit how far lending rates fall.
example: Say the RBI cuts the repo rate by 50 basis points and a bank's repo-linked home loan rate falls from 8.50% to 8.00% at the next reset. On a ₹50 lakh outstanding loan, the first year's interest falls by about ₹50 lakh × 0.50% = ₹25,000.
formula: Pass-through ratio = Change in lending rate / Change in policy rate

short: A central bank buying or selling foreign currency, usually US dollars, to steady or steer its own currency's exchange rate.
kid: If too many children want to swap their stickers for marbles, the swapping gets unfair. A grown-up with a big box of marbles steps in and hands some out so things stay calm.
detail: In FX intervention, a central bank trades its own currency against foreign currency to influence the exchange rate. Selling dollars from reserves supports the home currency; buying dollars restrains its rise and builds reserves. The RBI intervenes in the spot market, the onshore forward market and offshore non-deliverable forwards, and says it aims to curb excessive volatility rather than defend any particular level of the rupee. Intervention has side effects: selling dollars drains rupee liquidity from banks and buying adds it, so it is often offset through sterilisation. Reserves are finite, which is why traders watch the weekly reserves data; India's reserves fell by more than $100 billion between September 2021 and October 2022, partly from intervention and partly from valuation changes. Confusion to avoid: intervention smooths moves but rarely reverses a trend driven by interest-rate gaps or capital flows.
example: Say the RBI sells $2 billion to banks at ₹85 per dollar to slow a fall in the rupee. Banks pay $2,000,000,000 × 85 = ₹17,000 crore, so the RBI's dollar reserves fall by $2 billion and ₹17,000 crore of rupee liquidity leaves the banking system.
formula: Rupee liquidity impact = Dollars sold or bought × Exchange rate

short: A central bank offsetting the effect of its currency buying or selling on the money supply, usually by doing an opposite trade in bonds.
kid: If you pour an extra cup of water into a bowl, you can scoop one cup out the other side. The bowl stays just as full as before.
detail: When the RBI buys dollars to absorb capital inflows, it pays with newly created rupees, which adds to bank liquidity and could push down short-term rates and fuel inflation. Sterilisation offsets this: the RBI sells government bonds through open market operations, issues Market Stabilisation Scheme securities, absorbs funds through its deposit facilities or raises the cash reserve ratio. When it sells dollars, the reverse applies, and it may buy bonds to replace the drained liquidity. Sterilisation lets a central bank lean against currency moves without losing control of domestic interest rates, but it has costs. The interest paid on sterilisation instruments usually exceeds what reserves earn abroad, a quasi-fiscal cost, and keeping domestic rates high can attract still more inflows. Confusion to avoid: fully sterilised intervention leaves the money supply unchanged, so it moves the exchange rate mainly through signalling and portfolio effects.
example: Say the RBI buys $5 billion of inflows at ₹83 per dollar, creating $5,000,000,000 × 83 = ₹41,500 crore of new rupee liquidity. It then sells ₹41,500 crore of government bonds in open market operations, so reserves rise by $5 billion while rupee liquidity ends where it started.
formula: Liquidity to offset = Foreign currency bought or sold × Exchange rate

short: An Indian scheme where the government issues special bonds and bills only to soak up surplus bank money, with the proceeds frozen at the RBI.
kid: When too many sweets are lying around the classroom, the teacher collects some in a locked box. Nobody eats them; they are just kept away until things calm down.
detail: The Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) was set up in April 2004 under a memorandum between the Government of India and the RBI, when heavy dollar inflows meant the RBI was buying dollars and running short of government bonds to sell for sterilisation. Under MSS, the government issues treasury bills and dated securities, but the money raised sits in a separate MSS account with the RBI and cannot be spent; it only drains liquidity. The government bears the interest cost, which is why a ceiling is agreed with the RBI. MSS was used heavily in 2007-08 and again after demonetisation in November 2016, when the ceiling was raised to ₹6 lakh crore to absorb the surge in bank deposits. Newer tools such as the standing deposit facility have reduced the need for it. Confusion to avoid: MSS securities look like normal government borrowing but do not fund the fiscal deficit.
example: Say the government issues ₹20,000 crore of 91-day MSS bills at 6.5% a year. The ₹20,000 crore stays frozen at the RBI, and the government's interest cost is about ₹20,000 crore × 6.5% × 91 / 365 = ₹324 crore.
formula: Interest cost = Amount issued × Yield × Days / 365

short: A central bank's role of lending to sound banks that suddenly run short of cash in a crisis, when nobody else will.
kid: If everyone asks the lemonade stand for their coins back at once, its tin might be empty. A kind grown-up lends coins for a day, holding the stand's good jug as a promise.
detail: As lender of last resort, a central bank provides emergency liquidity to banks that are solvent but cannot meet sudden withdrawals, because their assets, such as loans and bonds, cannot be sold quickly at fair prices. Walter Bagehot's classic 1873 rule is to lend freely, against good collateral, at a penalty rate, so panic subsides without rewarding recklessness. The role exists because a run can sink even a healthy bank, and fear spreads to others. Examples include the Fed's lending in 2008 and after Silicon Valley Bank's collapse in 2023, and the RBI's special liquidity windows for mutual funds and NBFCs in 2008 and 2020. Confusion to avoid: lending against collateral to a solvent bank differs from rescuing an insolvent one, which needs fresh capital from shareholders, creditors or the government, as in the SBI-led reconstruction of Yes Bank in 2020.
example: Say ABC Bank faces ₹5,000 crore of withdrawals in two days but holds ₹8,000 crore of government bonds. If the central bank lends against them after a 10% haircut, ABC can borrow up to ₹8,000 crore × 90% = ₹7,200 crore, more than enough to pay depositors without a fire sale.
formula: Maximum borrowing = Collateral value × (1 - Haircut)

short: An agreement letting one central bank borrow another's currency, usually dollars, by swapping its own currency temporarily, so it can lend to banks at home.
kid: Two friends promise each other: if you ever run out of my colour of crayon, I will swap mine for yours, and we swap back later. It helps when someone suddenly needs a colour they don't have.
detail: In a central bank swap line, one central bank sells its currency to another in exchange for foreign currency, agreeing to reverse the trade on a set date at the same exchange rate, with the borrower paying interest. The borrowing central bank then lends the foreign currency to its own banks. Because so much global trade and borrowing is in dollars, Federal Reserve swap lines are critical in a crisis: they eased dollar shortages in 2008 and March 2020, and the Fed keeps standing lines with the ECB, Bank of Japan, Bank of England, Swiss National Bank and Bank of Canada. India relies on other arrangements, as of 2025 a bilateral swap arrangement with Japan of up to $75 billion, and the RBI itself offers swaps to SAARC central banks. Confusion to avoid: these are deals between central banks, not the cross-currency swaps companies use to hedge foreign debt.
example: Say the Fed swaps $10 billion with the ECB at $1.10 per euro. The ECB receives $10 billion and the Fed receives $10,000,000,000 / 1.10 = about €9.09 billion; at maturity they swap back at the same 1.10 rate, so neither faces exchange-rate risk, and the ECB pays the agreed interest.

short: The freedom of a central bank to set interest rates and run monetary policy without day-to-day pressure from the government or politicians.
kid: A referee in a football game has to make fair calls, even if a team captain shouts at them. If the captain could choose the calls, the game would not stay fair for long.
detail: Independence usually means operational freedom: the government may set the goal, such as an inflation target, but the central bank chooses how to reach it. The case for it: politicians are tempted to cut rates or print money before elections, which lifts growth briefly but leaves higher inflation; studies across countries link more independent central banks with lower, steadier inflation. Safeguards include long fixed terms for governors (14 years on the Fed's Board), protection from removal except for cause, and published decisions and votes. In India, Section 7 of the RBI Act lets the government give directions to the RBI after consulting the Governor; reports in 2018 that consultations under it had begun came shortly before Governor Urjit Patel resigned. Markets treat political pressure as a risk that can lift long-term yields. Confusion to avoid: independence does not mean freedom from accountability to parliament and the law.
example: Say investors start to fear that a government will push its central bank to cut rates before an election, and demand an extra 0.5 percentage point on 10-year government bonds. For a government borrowing ₹10 lakh crore a year, that adds ₹10 lakh crore × 0.5% = ₹5,000 crore a year in interest on each year's borrowing.

short: A central bank persuading banks to act in a certain way through meetings, letters and public statements, rather than through binding rules or rate changes.
kid: Instead of making a new rule, the teacher kindly asks the older children to share the swings. They listen because they respect her and know she could make a rule if needed.
detail: Moral suasion, sometimes called jawboning, is informal pressure: a governor meets bank chiefs, writes to them or makes speeches urging them to pass on rate cuts, curb lending to an overheated sector, lend more to small firms or avoid speculation. It works because banks know the central bank is also their regulator and could impose formal rules if ignored. The RBI has long used it, for example urging banks to pass policy rate cuts on to borrowers faster, or to tighten standards on unsecured loans before acting formally. It is quick, flexible and cheap, but its effect is hard to measure and can fade if banks see no follow-through. It also raises transparency concerns, since the pressure is not written down as rules. Confusion to avoid: moral suasion is advice backed by authority, not a legal order; formal tools such as directions, risk weights or reserve requirements are separate.
example: Say the RBI cuts the repo rate by 25 basis points but most banks lower their lending rates by only 10 basis points. The Governor meets bank chiefs and urges them to pass on the remaining 25 - 10 = 15 basis points to borrowers, without changing any rule.

short: Rules aimed at the safety of the whole financial system, such as limits on risky lending, rather than at the health of any single bank.
kid: A lifeguard doesn't just watch one swimmer; she watches the whole pool. If too many children crowd the deep end, she makes a rule so nobody gets into trouble together.
detail: Macroprudential policy targets systemic risk, the danger that problems hit many lenders at once, for example through a credit boom or a sector everyone is exposed to. Microprudential supervision asks whether each bank is safe; macroprudential policy asks whether the system is. Tools include countercyclical capital buffers, higher risk weights for booming loan categories, loan-to-value and debt-to-income caps, extra capital for systemically important banks and limits on foreign-currency borrowing. In November 2023 the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer loans and on bank lending to NBFCs by 25 percentage points, forcing lenders to hold more capital and slowing that lending; the NBFC increase was reversed from April 2025. India's loan-to-value caps on home and gold loans are other examples. These tools cool risky pockets without raising interest rates for everyone. Confusion to avoid: macroprudential tools manage financial-system risk, while monetary policy targets inflation, though the two interact.
example: Say a bank has ₹100 crore of personal loans and must hold capital of 11.5% of risk-weighted assets. When the risk weight rises from 100% to 125%, risk-weighted assets go from ₹100 crore to ₹125 crore, and required capital rises from ₹11.5 crore to ₹125 crore × 11.5% = ₹14.375 crore.
formula: Capital required = Loan amount × Risk weight × Minimum capital ratio

short: New money created by the central bank and handed directly to people or the government to spend, without ever having to be repaid.
kid: Imagine a helicopter flying over the park and dropping coins that never have to be given back. Everyone picks some up and runs to buy ice cream.
detail: Helicopter money comes from Milton Friedman's 1969 thought experiment of dropping cash from a helicopter. In practice it means a permanent, money-financed fiscal stimulus: the central bank creates money to fund transfers or tax cuts, and the money is never repaid. This differs from quantitative easing, where the central bank buys bonds that it can later sell or let mature, and from ordinary deficits financed by borrowing. Ben Bernanke's 2002 speech on preventing deflation earned him the nickname 'Helicopter Ben'. The pandemic revived the idea: cheques to households were funded by debt that central banks bought in bulk, close to but not quite a helicopter drop. It can lift spending when rates are at zero, but risks high inflation and erodes central bank independence. In India, automatic RBI financing of deficits ended in 1997, and the FRBM Act barred primary bond purchases from 2006, except in special cases.
example: Say a central bank permanently credits ₹5,000 to each of 10 crore households. That creates ₹5,000 × 10 crore = ₹50,000 crore of new money that no one has to repay, unlike a government loan or a bond bought under QE.

short: A twice-yearly RBI report assessing risks to India's financial system, including stress tests showing how banks would cope in a bad economy.
kid: Twice a year, a careful helper checks every tower of blocks in the playroom. She writes down which ones might wobble if someone bumps the table, so they can be fixed early.
detail: The RBI publishes its Financial Stability Report in June and December, reflecting the assessment of the Sub-Committee of the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) on risks to the financial system. It covers global and domestic macro risks, the health of banks, NBFCs, insurers and mutual funds, corporate and household debt, and links between institutions. Its most quoted section is the macro stress test, which projects banks' gross NPA ratio and capital adequacy over the next year under a baseline and adverse scenarios. Markets read it for early warnings, for instance about rapid growth in unsecured loans. Other central banks publish similar reports: the Fed and Bank of England twice a year, and the ECB its Financial Stability Review. Confusion to avoid: the FSR is a risk assessment, not a rule; it does not change rates or regulations itself, though it can foreshadow macroprudential action.
example: Say an FSR projects that banks' capital ratio would fall from 16.0% to 12.5% under a severe stress scenario, a drop of 3.5 percentage points. That would still be above the 11.5% minimum including the capital conservation buffer under the RBI's rules as of 2025, so the system would remain adequately capitalised.

short: The highest level a central bank's policy rate is expected to reach in a cycle of rate hikes, before it pauses or starts cutting.
kid: When you climb a slide's ladder, you go up one step at a time. The very top step, where the climbing stops, is the one everyone was trying to guess.
detail: The terminal rate is where a tightening cycle ends: the peak policy rate. Markets estimate it from interest-rate futures and overnight index swaps, and central banks hint at it through forward guidance and, at the Fed, the dot plot. It matters because bond yields, especially at two to five years, price the whole expected path of rates, not just the next move; a higher expected terminal rate lifts borrowing costs and weighs on valuations even before the hikes happen. In the 2022-23 cycle the Fed's range peaked at 5.25-5.50% in July 2023 and the RBI's repo rate at 6.50% in February 2023. Analysts sometimes use the term for the low point of a cutting cycle too. Confusion to avoid: the terminal rate is not the neutral rate; central banks usually take rates above neutral at the peak, and the terminal rate is known for certain only in hindsight.
example: Between May 2022 and February 2023 the RBI raised the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50%, a total of 6.50% - 4.00% = 2.50 percentage points, or 250 basis points. The 6.50% level, held through 2023 and 2024, was the terminal rate of that cycle.

short: The lasting surplus or shortage of cash in India's banking system, excluding short-lived swings such as moves in the government's balance at the RBI.
kid: Some water in a pond comes from a quick shower and dries up by evening. The water that stays for weeks is the part you can count on.
detail: Banking system liquidity in India moves daily: tax payments drain cash into the government's account at the RBI, and government spending later releases it. Durable, or core, liquidity strips out these temporary swings to show the underlying surplus or deficit, commonly estimated as the net position under the RBI's liquidity adjustment facility plus the government's cash balance with the RBI. It is driven by slower forces: currency in circulation, the RBI's foreign exchange purchases or sales, open market operations, longer-term repos and changes in the cash reserve ratio. A durable deficit keeps money market rates above the repo rate and weakens transmission, so the RBI adds liquidity through OMO purchases, forex buy/sell swaps or CRR cuts, such as the 100 basis point CRR cut phased in from September to November 2025. Confusion to avoid: daily LAF data can show a deficit even when durable liquidity is in surplus.
example: Say the RBI is absorbing a net ₹1.5 lakh crore through its liquidity window while the government holds ₹2 lakh crore of cash at the RBI after a tax collection. Durable liquidity is about ₹1.5 lakh crore + ₹2 lakh crore = ₹3.5 lakh crore in surplus, because the government's cash will flow back to banks as it spends.
formula: Durable liquidity ≈ Net LAF position + Government cash balances with the RBI

short: A Federal Reserve facility that lends cash overnight to banks and dealers against safe US bonds at a set rate, capping spikes in short-term rates.
kid: If a shop suddenly needs coins at night, a helper next door is always open. The shop leaves a safe toy as a promise, borrows coins and swaps back in the morning.
detail: The Fed set up the standing repo facility (SRF) in July 2021, after episodes such as September 2019, when overnight repo rates briefly touched about 10% because reserves had become scarce. In daily operations, primary dealers and eligible banks can borrow cash overnight from the Fed by selling it Treasuries, agency debt or agency mortgage-backed securities and agreeing to buy them back the next day. The minimum bid rate is set at the top of the fed funds target range, so the SRF works as a ceiling: no one should need to pay much more than that for repo funding. Use picked up around month- and quarter-ends in 2025 as quantitative tightening drained reserves. It complements the ON RRP facility, which sets the floor. Confusion to avoid: the SRF injects cash, unlike the RBI's standing deposit facility, which absorbs it; India's ceiling tool is the marginal standing facility.
example: Say a primary dealer borrows $1 billion overnight from the SRF at a minimum bid rate of 4.50% while private repo trades at 4.60%. It pays $1,000,000,000 × 4.50% / 360 = $125,000 instead of about $127,778 in the market, saving about $2,778.
formula: Overnight interest = Amount borrowed × SRF rate × 1/360

short: A Fed approach, used from 2020 to 2025, of aiming for 2% average inflation over time, allowing overshoots after periods below 2%.
kid: If you got too few sweets on Monday and Tuesday, a fair parent might give you a few extra on Wednesday and Thursday. Over the whole week, it evens out.
detail: The Federal Reserve adopted flexible average inflation targeting (FAIT) in August 2020, announced by Jerome Powell at Jackson Hole after a review prompted by years of inflation below 2% and rates stuck near zero. Instead of letting bygones be bygones, the Fed said that after periods of inflation persistently below 2% it would aim for inflation moderately above 2% for some time, so the average returned to target and expectations stayed anchored. It also said it would respond to 'shortfalls' from maximum employment rather than deviations, signalling no pre-emptive hikes. Critics argue this delayed the response to the 2021-22 inflation surge. In August 2025 the Fed's next framework review dropped the averaging and shortfalls language and returned to flexible inflation targeting. Confusion to avoid: FAIT never had a formula or a fixed averaging window; it was deliberately loose. India's framework targets inflation directly, not an average.
example: Say inflation averaged 1.5% for four years. To bring the eight-year average back to 2%, inflation would need to run at 2.5% for the next four years, because (4 × 1.5% + 4 × 2.5%) / 8 = 2%.
formula: Average inflation = Sum of yearly inflation rates / Number of years

short: The RBI's outstanding contracts to buy or sell US dollars at future dates, which show how much future dollar supply it has already promised.
kid: Today you promise your friend you will give her five marbles next month. You still have them now, but you should not count them as yours to spend.
detail: Besides spot trades, the RBI intervenes through forwards and swaps: it may sell dollars for delivery months ahead, or do buy/sell swaps that add dollars now and commit it to sell them later. The net of these commitments is its forward book, published monthly in the RBI Bulletin by maturity bucket. A large net short position means the RBI has promised to deliver dollars in future, so analysts subtract it from headline reserves to judge true firepower. It also reveals the scale of intervention: the net short position climbed above $80 billion in early 2025, a record, as the RBI defended the rupee and used swaps to inject rupee liquidity. Forwards support the rupee without an immediate drop in reserves, but create obligations that must later be met or rolled over. Confusion to avoid: the forward book is not part of reserves; it is a claim on them.
example: Say the RBI holds $650 billion of headline reserves and has a net short forward position of $80 billion. Reserves net of forward commitments are $650 billion - $80 billion = $570 billion, a more cautious measure of how much it could spend defending the rupee.
formula: Net reserves = Headline forex reserves - Net short forward position

short: The RBI's rulebook for how much income it keeps as a safety buffer against risks and how much surplus it passes to the government.
kid: At the end of the lemonade stand's summer, the children first put some coins in a rainy-day jar. Whatever is left over goes to the grown-ups who lent them the stand.
detail: The RBI's income comes mostly from interest on its bond and foreign currency holdings, and Section 47 of the RBI Act requires it to pass surplus profits to the government after provisions. The Economic Capital Framework decides those provisions. After public disagreement over the RBI's reserves, a committee led by former Governor Bimal Jalan recommended in 2019 that the Contingent Risk Buffer, the RBI's equity cushion against monetary, financial-stability and credit risks, be kept at 5.5% to 6.5% of the balance sheet. That allowed a transfer of about ₹1.76 lakh crore in August 2019. In 2025 the RBI widened the range to 4.5% to 7.5%, kept the buffer at 7.5% and paid ₹2.69 lakh crore for 2024-25, a record at the time. The payout matters for the fiscal deficit and bond markets. Confusion to avoid: unrealised gains on forex and gold sit in revaluation accounts and are not paid out.
example: Say the RBI's balance sheet is ₹60 lakh crore and its board sets the Contingent Risk Buffer at 6.5%. The buffer must be ₹60 lakh crore × 6.5% = ₹3.9 lakh crore; if it stands at ₹3.6 lakh crore, ₹30,000 crore of the year's income goes to topping it up before the surplus is transferred.
formula: Surplus transferred = Net income - Provisions needed to bring the Contingent Risk Buffer to its target
